items.gist: The passage describes resting in the supreme with all-pervading fullness, where consciousness appears as 'I' in anuttara vimarśa beyond prior activity.
It traces the arising of cidvimarśa as parāhaṃkṛt, then the twelve-sunned illumination and sixteen-mooned visarga releasing amṛta into the fire of consciousness.
The divine amṛta nourishes the goddesses of consciousness; visarga is identified with kulanāyikā, and the universe is said to be made of that visarga.
The practitioner worships and offers the saṃjīvanī kalā, then enters the heart through nāḍī vibration, contraction, and all-self pervasion.
Friction of lunar and solar kalās in the agni-soma abode makes visargānanda arise; the yogī rests in the heart of the yoginī.
Seeing the universe as non-dual wonder, one abandons external-internal distinction, attains nirvṛti, and expands consciousness through the saṃvid-akṣara cakra.
The knowable dissolves in the fire of consciousness and then in the triangular śakti-fire, where the yogī rests in bindu and saṃhāra-bīja.
Consciousness-spanda operates through three śaktis with contraction and expansion; even without contraction, inner focus with outer sight attains the supreme state.
The distinctive spanda of svātantrya arises, and the yogī rests there, since siddhis arise through identity with their respective forms.
The divine sense-group makes the universe one's own self; in mahāsāhasa union all activity dissolves, and the thoughtless seer attains consciousness.
The passage quotes Parameśa on entering mantra-bhūmi: upward movement in the central nāḍī, beyond visarga, gives great light and knowledge.
One enters the city through mātrāvṛtti, then contemplates and enters the space-syllable khaṃ, abandoning and ascending through khaṃ.
One meditates on inner bhāva, restrains bhāva-abhāva, and recognizes the three śaktis; khaṃ is taught tenfold with uccāra.
One awakens dhāma by dhāma, makes dhāma reach its end, and pierces through bhedas; this is the āṇava entry method.
The tenfold rāva is described, and the great yogī who conquers rāva can enter another body and attain supreme pervasion.
The rāviṇī dissolves into rāva; through fullness, deha-less absorption, and momentary samāveśa, pluti arises.
Bodily looseness produces kampa; before consciousness is rooted, nidrā occurs, then ghūrṇi as mahāvyāpti when non-self is seen as self.
Self-identification with body is bondage and its dissolution liberation; the fivefold set of ānanda, kampa, nidrā, ghūrṇi, and mahāvyāpti is stated.
When the yogī enters, he forcibly attains cakreśatva; just as a body seized by supreme consciousness can still act, entry into a cakra can occur.
The ānandacakra is located at the kanda, with kampa, hṛt-tālu, nidrā, and ghūrṇi as ūrdhvakuṇḍalī; this is clearly stated in the Mantraiśirasa view.
The avyakta liṅga, undivided from Śiva-śakti, is where the universe dissolves and is known within the mātrā; it is the mark of full-powered Bhairava-consciousness.
The vyakta liṅga is consciousness-natured spanda; from the vyakta comes siddhi, from vyakta-avyakta liberation, and from avyakta initial power.
The vyakta naraliṅga is where the universe is offered; when that dissolves, the avyakta remains, and in that avyakta one rests, not in the anuttara abode.
One spanda has a threefold division into vyakta, vyakta-avyakta, and avyakta; one should always remain in this liṅga, devoted to pūjā and rest.
